content.jointProblem: How can Lex Automatika add script-aware normalisation to KlozuraPro's PostgreSQL full-text search pipeline so that Latin- and Cyrillic-script queries retrieve the same Serbian contract documents, including mixed-script documents, without noticeably increasing query latency? The project would compare indexing-time, query-time and combined transliteration/normalisation strategies on representative contract and query samples.

rationale.text: Dragišić has a research background specifically in morphological processing of legal Serbian texts.

sources.quote: dissertation on morphological tagging of legal texts in Serbian

rationale.text: He has prior legal-tech consultancy experience in morphological normalisation for Serbian contract documents.

sources.quote: advising on morphological normalisation and entity detection for Serbian contract documents

rationale.text: He has built a large domain-specific morphological lexicon for legal Serbian, directly relevant to robust handling of inflected and specialised contract vocabulary.

sources.quote: The resulting lexicon contains 87,400 lemma–paradigm pairs and 620,000 fully inflected word forms

rationale.text: His South Slavic cross-lingual work has used romanised transliteration as part of a shared feature representation, giving him relevant exposure to script transfer issues.

sources.quote: shared feature representation built from romanised transliteration, language-independent character embeddings, and shared morphological clusters

rationale.text: His project work has produced openly released Serbian language resources, matching the resource-building component he is best approached for.

sources.quote: All outputs were deposited in the CLARIN.SI repository under open licences.

risks: The transliteration evidence in the researcher's material is from cross-lingual named-entity recognition feature representation, not from PostgreSQL full-text search; transfer to indexing-time or query-time normalisation is untested and should be the first experiment.

The company already notes dialect-dependent edge cases where the same Latin sequence maps to different Cyrillic letters; the researcher's material does not show which convention KlozuraPro clients expect.
Mixed-script document retrieval is not directly covered by the cited resources; the legal lexicon and corpora do not prove robustness on documents mixing Cyrillic and Latin within the same contract.
Researcher availability is unknown, so capacity for a joint project cannot be assumed until confirmed.
Lex Automatika has one backend engineer for up to six weeks and capacity for roughly one external project at a time, which may constrain implementation and evaluation scope.

The researcher's caution about exclusive data transfer and requirement for open licensing of publicly funded corpus outputs may conflict with client contract data, server logs or proprietary platform constraints.
questions: Can Strahinja Dragišić confirm his availability and capacity for a joint project, and whether he would also consider an industrial PhD format?
Which Serbian Latin–Cyrillic transliteration convention or conventions must KlozuraPro support, especially for dialect-dependent edge cases?
Can Lex Automatika provide anonymised mixed-script contract samples and query-log samples under agreed data terms for evaluation?
What is the current search-latency baseline and the acceptable latency budget for the new normalisation step?
Which pipeline points may be changed: PostgreSQL indexing/query functions, application-layer query rewriting, or both?
Can publicly funded corpus outputs be openly licensed, and what restrictions apply to client contract data and server logs?
